output.title: Kimchi Club Monthly: Sour Smell, Simple Fixes, and a Fresh Batch Idea
output.body:
This month’s recipe idea: try a quick radish kimchi. Slice radish into matchsticks, salt lightly, add garlic, ginger, gochugaru, and a little fish sauce or soy sauce, then pack tightly into a clean jar. Press until the brine rises and leave room at the top. Taste after a few days, then chill when it reaches the tang you like.

Troubleshooting tip: a sour smell often means fermentation is moving along, not that something is wrong. If the jar smells sharply sour, check for enough liquid, a tight pack, and cool storage once it is active. If the smell is pleasant and tangy, it may simply be developing faster than expected.

Reader question: Why does my jar smell too sour? Answer: usually because it fermented warm or for longer than planned. That can happen quickly in summer. Next time, taste earlier, keep the jar cooler, and move it to the fridge once the flavor hits your sweet spot.

output.decisionQuestion: Should Kimchi Club keep the reader Q&A focused on flavor/timing only, or add a brief note about checking visible signs like bubbling and jar seal?
options: Add visible signs and a short storage reminder

Hi Kimchi Club friends, here’s a cozy jar check-in.

Recipe idea: quick cucumber kimchi with garlic, ginger, and scallions for a bright, crunchy batch.

Troubleshooting tip: if a jar smells too sour, it may simply be fermenting fast in a warm spot. Try moving it cooler next time and tasting earlier.

Reader question: “Why does my jar smell so sour?” A sour aroma is often part of the process, especially as time goes on. If it smells rotten instead of sour, throw the jar out.
